title: What training do mortgage brokers need for the best interests duty?
description: The NCCP Act best interests duty for Australian mortgage brokers, ASIC RG 273 and RG 206 qualification and CPD settings, and what industry bodies add on top.
shortAnswer: Australian mortgage brokers must act in the best interests of consumers and prioritize consumers' interests in a conflict, under Part 3-5A of the National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009, in force since January 1, 2021. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) expects brokers giving third party home loan assistance to hold at least a Certificate IV in Finance and Mortgage Broking and complete 20 hours of continuing professional development (CPD) each year.
keyTakeaways: The best interests duty is in sections 158LA (licensees) and 158LE (credit representatives) of the National Credit Act; the conflict priority rule is in sections 158LB and 158LF.
The obligations started on January 1, 2021, after ASIC deferred the original July 1, 2020 start by six months because of COVID-19.
Under section 158LE(2) and 158LF(2) a licensee must take reasonable steps to make its broker representatives comply, and ASIC's first expectation is that brokers are adequately trained and competent.

ASIC's RG 206 sets the Certificate IV in Finance and Mortgage Broking and 20 CPD hours a year for representatives and responsible managers in third party home lending. The Diploma is not an ASIC requirement.
Industry association rules sit on top: the MFAA, for example, requires members to hold the Diploma within 12 months of joining and complete 30 CPD hours a year.
appliesTo: Mortgage brokers as defined in section 15B of the National Credit Act, whatever their job title
Australian credit licensees that authorize mortgage broker credit representatives, including aggregators
Responsible managers of credit licensees that provide third party home loan credit assistance
Mortgage managers who meet the section 15B definition

sections.heading: What does the best interests duty require of mortgage brokers?

blocks.text: A mortgage broker must act in the best interests of the consumer when providing credit assistance, and must give priority to the consumer's interests where the broker knows, or reasonably ought to know, of a conflict with the interests of the licensee, the representative, or their associates. These obligations are in Part 3-5A of the [National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2009A00134/latest/text), whose sections 158LA and 158LE are headed "must act in the best interests of the consumer" for licensees and credit representatives respectively.

ASIC's [RG 273 Mortgage brokers: Best interests duty](https://asic.gov.au/regulatory-resources/find-a-document/regulatory-guides/rg-273-mortgage-brokers-best-interests-duty/), issued on June 24, 2020, explains how ASIC assesses compliance. The duty arose from Recommendation 1.2 of the Royal Commission into Misconduct in the Banking, Superannuation and Financial Services Industry (RG 273.1 to RG 273.2), and it applies only to credit regulated by the National Credit Act, meaning credit for personal, domestic or household purposes or for buying or improving residential investment property (RG 273.5).

A person is a mortgage broker if they carry on a business of providing credit assistance for credit secured by mortgages over residential property, are not the credit provider for most of those contracts, and deal with more than one credit provider (s15B, RG 273.7). The label does not matter: a mortgage manager meeting those criteria is caught (RG 273.8).

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the National Credit Act compilation of July 1, 2026, RG 273 (June 2020) and RG 206 (April 2020, updated October 2022) as at November 2026. Industry association rules quoted are those published by the association at that date and can change without legislative amendment.

sections.heading: When did the best interests duty start?

blocks.text: Brokers and relevant credit licensees have had to comply since January 1, 2021 (RG 273.4). The obligations were inserted by the Financial Sector Reform (Hayne Royal Commission Response: Protecting Consumers (2019 Measures)) Act 2020 and were due to start on July 1, 2020, but ASIC Credit (Deferral of Mortgage Broker Obligations) Instrument 2020/487 gave a six month exemption because of COVID-19.

For training programs the date matters mainly for file reviews. Files for credit assistance given from January 1, 2021 must show best interests reasoning as well as responsible lending inquiries, so a training needs analysis drawn from earlier files can understate the gap.

sections.heading: What must the credit licensee do to make brokers comply?

blocks.text: Credit licensees must take reasonable steps to ensure their credit representatives who are mortgage brokers comply with the best interests duty and the conflict priority rule (s158LE(2) and 158LF(2), RG 273.173). ASIC says this obligation is preventive, so a licensee can fail to take reasonable steps even if no broker has yet breached the duty (RG 273.177 to RG 273.178).
RG 273.179 lists what ASIC generally expects. Licensees should:

items: ensure their mortgage brokers are adequately trained and competent, applying the general training and competence requirements in RG 206;
provide systems, guidelines and other materials so brokers understand and comply with their best interests obligations;
monitor compliance, with method and frequency varying by the licensee's circumstances; and
ensure records are kept that show both the broker's compliance and the reasonable steps the licensee has taken.

blocks.text: ASIC's Example 19 in RG 273 is directly about training. A licensee that learns one broker has breached the duty, but makes no attempt to educate its other brokers or check how widespread the behavior is, is likely to have failed to take reasonable steps; additional training is named as a reasonable preventive step. This makes post breach retraining part of the legal standard, not an optional extra, and the guide on [updating training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change) applies equally to updates triggered by a breach.

sections.heading: What qualifications and CPD does ASIC expect of mortgage brokers?

blocks.text: ASIC expects representatives who provide third party home loan credit assistance to hold at least a Certificate IV in Finance and Mortgage Broking and to complete at least 20 hours of CPD each year (RG 206.23(a)). The guide explains why: "poorly informed assistance leading to poor decisions about home loans could potentially jeopardise ownership of the family home" (RG 206.24).

blocks.text: For responsible managers, RG 206.71 says the 20 hour requirement is set out in a license condition that also requires the licensee to keep a record of CPD undertaken each year. CPD should cover product and industry developments and compliance training on new regulatory requirements (RG 206.72). Countable activities include seminars and conferences, online tutorials or quizzes on developments within the last year, recorded seminars up to 10 hours a year, and internal training on systems and policies, provided internal training is not the majority of hours. ASIC generally does not regard private study as adequate CPD (RG 206.73).

Section 47(1)(f) of the National Credit Act, which carries the organizational competence obligation, is a civil penalty provision. RG 206 gives maximums of the greater of 5,000 penalty units or three times the benefit for individuals, and up to 50,000 penalty units, three times the benefit or a turnover based amount for bodies corporate (RG 206.16 to RG 206.18). The equivalent rules for AFS licensees are explained on the [RG 105 responsible managers page](/regulations/asic-rg-105-organisational-competence).

sections.heading: Which broker education rules come from ASIC and which from industry bodies?

blocks.text: ASIC's settings are the Certificate IV and 20 CPD hours in RG 206; the Diploma of Finance and Mortgage Broking Management and higher CPD hours are membership requirements of industry associations, not ASIC rules. Treating the two as one causes errors in both directions: a licensee may assume the Diploma satisfies the best interests duty, or may record association CPD without tying it to the credit obligations RG 206.72 expects CPD to cover.

As one example, the Mortgage & Finance Association of Australia (MFAA) [key requirements page](https://www.mfaa.com.au/become-a-broker/key-requirements) says members need the Diploma of Finance and Mortgage Broking Management, that members joining with only the Certificate IV must complete the Diploma within 12 months of joining to renew, and that members must complete 30 CPD hours a year plus an annual Compliance Refresher. Other associations publish their own rules, which should be checked directly. Where an aggregator or employer makes association membership a condition of engagement, those rules apply to the broker through that arrangement, not through ASIC.

sections.heading: How should a licensee map best interests obligations to training evidence?

blocks.text: The most useful evidence links each step of RG 273 to an observable broker behavior and to a file record that proves it. RG 273.165 lists the records ASIC generally expects on each file, and RG 273.167 includes training materials, training attendance records and call scripts as evidence of the compliance systems used. The table is an original, illustrative mapping built from those paragraphs; ASIC has not endorsed it.

blocks.text: A scenario based [competency assessment](/glossary/competency-assessment) is stronger evidence than attendance alone, because RG 273's examples turn on judgment about what a consumer actually needs. The guide to [setting up verification of competency](/guides/how-to-set-up-verification-of-competency) shows how to link a file review to a recorded pass or fail decision.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures the best interests obligations, the RG 206 settings and any association rules as separate, linked layers, so each assessment item shows which source requires it. When ASIC guidance or an association rule changes, the affected broker assessments are identified from the framework, and the licensee's reasonable steps record shows which version each broker was assessed against.

faqs.q: Does ASIC require mortgage brokers to hold the Diploma?
faqs.a: No. RG 206 sets the Certificate IV in Finance and Mortgage Broking as the minimum for representatives and responsible managers in third party home lending. The Diploma of Finance and Mortgage Broking Management is required by industry associations such as the MFAA as a condition of membership.

faqs.q: How many CPD hours do mortgage brokers need?
faqs.a: ASIC expects at least 20 hours of CPD each year for brokers giving third party home loan credit assistance. The MFAA requires its members to complete 30 hours a year plus an annual Compliance Refresher, so a broker who is an MFAA member works to the higher figure.

faqs.q: Does the best interests duty apply to business loans?
faqs.a: RG 273 says the obligations apply only to credit regulated by the National Credit Act, which is credit for personal, domestic or household purposes or for buying or improving residential investment property. Credit wholly for business purposes is generally outside that scope.

faqs.q: Can an aggregator rely on brokers' own CPD?
faqs.a: The licensee that authorizes the broker must still take reasonable steps under sections 158LE(2) and 158LF(2), which ASIC says includes ensuring brokers are adequately trained and competent and monitoring compliance. Broker attested CPD can be part of the evidence, but monitoring and file reviews are also expected.

faqs.q: How long should best interests records be kept?
faqs.a: RG 273 does not set a single period. It says retention may depend on the loan term, any interest only period and whether the consumer refinances, and warns that keeping records for a short time risks being unable to show compliance.
